days.title: Summit push: Emerald Peak, Southeast Ridge

schedule.label: Leave camp
schedule.detail: Light daypack; crampons/axe carried if snow lingers in the gullies.

schedule.label: Reach the ~7,800 ft bench
schedule.detail: Below Emerald's southeast face; route-finding through slabby, choss-prone terrain.

schedule.label: Summit Emerald Peak (8,419 ft)
schedule.detail: Class 2-3 scrambling, minimal exposure but loose rock near the top.

schedule.label: Optional side trip to Saska Peak
schedule.detail: Common link-up since it shares the same bench; adds ~2 hrs round trip.

schedule.label: Back at camp
schedule.detail: Rest, refill water, prep for the hike out.

days.objective: Climb Emerald Peak and return to camp

days.note: Break camp and reverse the approach trail. The return typically goes faster than day 1 since the route-finding and creek crossing are now familiar; most parties are back at the vehicle by early-to-mid afternoon.
days.title: Hike out
days.objective: Return to the North Fork Entiat trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A standard 3-day, 2-night backpack: roughly 22 miles round trip with about 5,300 ft of total gain, most of it on the long approach; parties commonly link nearby Saska Peak (and sometimes Cardinal Peak, on a 4th day) onto the same basin camp since all three summits share the same approach.

road.name: FR 5606 (final 3 miles) via Entiat River Road/County Rd 19 to FR 51
road.status: Mostly graded gravel; generally passable for passenger cars in dry conditions with a couple of rough or dry-crossing sections, though high clearance is recommended. East-Cascades forest roads here wash out periodically — check the current road report with the Entiat Ranger District before driving. Closed: the Little Giant Fire closure (Okanogan-Wenatchee order 06-17-07-2026-40, in effect since September 3, 2026 and through October 31, 2026 unless lifted sooner) closes FR 5606 and the North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437. Check with the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest before you go.
road.driveNote: From the town of Entiat on US-97A, follow Entiat River Road (County Rd 19) north/west; it becomes FR 51 around mile 27, continue to mile 32.3, then turn onto FR 5606 and drive 3 more miles to its end at the North Fork Entiat Trailhead (3,940 ft).

itinerary.cal: The White Chuck River Road (FR 23) is closed to vehicles from milepost 3.7 after flood damage, so the approach starts at the North Fork Sauk trailhead instead; the Kennedy Glacier toe (crumbling boulders on ice) is described as the most hazardous section of the route in multiple reports.

days.note: From the North Fork Sauk trailhead (the White Chuck trailhead is cut off by the FR 23 closure at milepost 3.7), take the North Fork Sauk Trail to the PCT and follow it north over Red Pass to the Glacier Creek camps, then up to a camp on Kennedy Creek Bench near the toe of the Kennedy Glacier moraine.
days.title: Approach to Kennedy Creek Bench camp
days.objective: Reach camp at ~6,200 ft

days.note: A long, full-value day: climb the wide, moderately-crevassed Kennedy Glacier to the summit, then descend via Frostbite Ridge and the Vista Glacier back down to the lower Kennedy Glacier, regaining camp in the evening.
days.title: Summit via Kennedy Glacier, descend via Frostbite Ridge

schedule.label: Leave Kennedy Creek Bench
schedule.detail: Switch to boots/crampons at the crumbling, boulder-strewn toe of the glacier — a notably hazardous section.

schedule.label: Summit
schedule.detail: Via the wide-open Kennedy Glacier, then a rock-on-ice step and waterfall traverse lower down.

schedule.label: Down Frostbite Ridge and the Vista Glacier
schedule.detail: Past the 'Rabbit Ears' rock formation, then down the Vista Glacier to the lower Kennedy Glacier.

schedule.label: Back at camp
schedule.detail: 5.5 hr descent from the summit; plan headlamps for a late finish.

days.objective: Summit Glacier Peak (10,541 ft) and loop back to camp via a different glacier

days.note: Break camp and hike back down to the trailhead.
days.title: Hike out
days.objective: Return to trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A 3-day trip (~51 miles, roughly 15,900 ft gain) from the North Fork Sauk start, and every day of it is very long; plan a 4th or 5th day to split the walk in and the walk out.

road.name: North Fork Sauk Road / Sloan Creek Road (FR 49)
road.status: Gravel, with rough and washed-out sections; medium or high clearance is recommended and a low-clearance car may not clear them.
road.driveNote: The White Chuck Road (FR 23) approach to the old White Chuck River Trailhead is closed to vehicles from milepost 3.7 to its end for flood damage; check current status with the Darrington Ranger District.
road.seasonalGate: The Mountain Loop Highway's Deer Creek to Bedal section is gated through the winter and typically reopens in mid-May; FR 49 can hold snow into early summer in heavy years.

itinerary.cal: Also a seasonal snow climb (roughly January-May); check Longmire/Stevens Canyon Road gate hours before committing to a start time, and expect deeper/softer snow than the Zipper depending on aspect and recent weather.

days.note: Same approach as the Zipper via Stevens Canyon Road/Tatoosh Creek, but continue up the wider, more forgiving couloir just right of the Zipper to a notch in the west ridge. It's generally lower-commitment than the Zipper (often no roping needed in good nick), though it can hold deep, sluffy snow that slows the ascent. Descend via a non-technical line rather than down-climbing the couloir.
days.title: Car-to-car climb of the Fly couloir

schedule.label: Leave Reflection Lakes pullout
schedule.detail: Similar approach timing to the Zipper, roughly 45-75 minutes to the couloir base.

schedule.label: Climb the Fly
schedule.detail: Widens the higher you go; trail-breaking in fresh/deep snow can roughly double this leg.

schedule.label: Reach the west ridge notch and summit
schedule.detail: Short scramble from the top of the couloir.

schedule.label: Descend a non-technical line
schedule.detail: Most parties walk off rather than reversing the couloir.

days.objective: Climb the Fly, the broader/easier of Lane Peak's two main couloirs, to the west ridge

itinerary.totalNote: A single day comparable to the Zipper: roughly 5-6 hours and 1,500 ft car-to-car, sometimes paired with the Zipper in the same outing by strong parties.

road.name: Narada Falls parking lot (Paradise road) / Stevens Canyon Road
road.status: Narada Falls lot plowed and open year-round; Stevens Canyon Rd unplowed in winter
road.driveNote: Approach via Narada Falls in winter/spring; Reflection Lake is a shorter option once Stevens Canyon Rd opens for summer.
road.seasonalGate: Stevens Canyon Rd typically opens late June, closes with first significant snow (usually early-mid October)

itinerary.cal: Snow can linger on the upper ridge and summit block into July, so many early-season parties carry an ice axe; the Mountain Loop Highway trailhead access can also be affected by seasonal road/washout closures, worth checking before driving in.

days.note: A long, strenuous single-day scramble: forested trail past Lake Metan, then talus and wildflower meadows up to Stujack Pass, followed by a Class 2-3 ridge scramble (crux is a ~30-ft stepped chimney) to the summit block. Nearly all parties do this car-to-car with a day pack rather than camping.
days.title: Car-to-car summit day

schedule.label: Leave trailhead
schedule.detail: Mt. Pugh Trail #644 climbs gently through forest.

schedule.label: Pass Lake Metan (3,260 ft)
schedule.detail: Last reliable water source before the pass.

schedule.label: Reach Stujack Pass (~5,750 ft)
schedule.detail: Trail steepens through talus and meadows; enter Glacier Peak Wilderness.

schedule.label: Class 2-3 ridge scramble
schedule.detail: Route follows the ridge around the head of a small glacial remnant to the crux chimney.

schedule.label: Summit (7,201 ft)
schedule.detail: Sweeping views of Glacier Peak, Sloan, Baker, Shuksan, and Rainier.

schedule.label: Back at trailhead
schedule.detail: Descend the same line; watch cairns carefully through the scramble section.

days.objective: Summit Mount Pugh via Stujack Pass

itinerary.totalNote: A single long day: roughly 8-11 hours car-to-car for fit parties, ~11 miles round trip with about 5,300 ft of gain, no camping involved.

road.name: Mountain Loop Highway to Forest Road 2095 (FR-2095)
road.status: Paved Mountain Loop Highway to the FR-2095 turnoff, then a gravel spur about 1.5 miles to the trailhead
road.driveNote: Turn onto FR-2095 roughly 12.5 miles south of Darrington (signed); Darrington Ranger District can confirm road/gate status at (360) 436-1155.
road.seasonalGate: FR-2095 itself is gated Oct 16–Jun 1 for wildlife protection (Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie NF); separate Mountain Loop Highway winter closures may also apply.

itinerary.cal: Off-trail approach is brushy and best done once most snow has melted off the lower slopes, roughly mid-July through September; the Cascade River Road access is seasonal (typically gated/closed in winter).

days.note: From the Kindy Ridge trailhead on FR 1570 off the Cascade River Road, follow the blocked/overgrown road then a steep, unmaintained way-trail up Kindy Ridge, staying east of the 5,116' knoll and continuing along Kindy-Found Ridge to a basin camp near Cyclone Pond (~5,450') or the Found Lakes. This is entirely off-trail route-finding through brush and steep timber for the upper portion.
days.title: Approach to high camp
days.objective: Reach a basecamp in the Found Lake / Cyclone Pond basin below the Snowking–Mutchler ridge

days.note: From camp, traverse south along the connecting ridge/basin terrain toward Mutchler Peak, the alpine high point of Snowking's long southeast ridge. Expect class 2-3 scrambling on the final summit block with route-finding over talus and possible snow patches through early summer; return to the same camp by the same line.
days.title: Summit push to Mutchler Peak

schedule.label: Leave high camp
schedule.detail: Alpine start to have good snow/rock conditions and margin for route-finding.

schedule.label: Gain the connecting ridge
schedule.detail: Traverse basin and ridge terrain toward Mutchler's summit block.

schedule.label: Summit Mutchler Peak (7,150')
schedule.detail: Final scramble is class 2-3; watch for loose rock.

schedule.label: Back at high camp
schedule.detail: Reverse the ridge traverse and descent to camp.

days.objective: Climb Mutchler Peak (7,150') and return to high camp

days.note: Break camp and reverse the day 1 route back down Kindy-Found Ridge and the way-trail to the road end. Mostly downhill but still slow, brushy off-trail travel with a full pack.
days.title: Hike out
days.objective: Return to the Kindy Ridge trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A 3-day trip for most parties (in / summit / out): roughly 15-18 miles round trip with about 6,500 ft of cumulative gain, nearly all of it off-trail; strong, experienced parties familiar with the terrain sometimes compress this to 2 days.

itinerary.cal: Holden Village has been closed to vehicles and hikers due to storm damage through at least summer 2026 - confirm current access status and the Lady of the Lake boat/shuttle schedule before planning this trip, since the return connection is a tight same-day window.

days.note: Access to this remote Glacier Peak Wilderness peak starts with the Lady of the Lake passenger ferry from Chelan to Lucerne, then a shuttle bus to Holden Village. From there it's an 8+ mile trail hike up Railroad Creek to camp at Lower Lyman Lake, gaining about 2,400 ft.
days.title: Boat/bus access + backpack to Lyman Lakes

schedule.label: Board Lady of the Lake ferry in Chelan
Arrive Lucerne, transfer to Holden Village shuttle
Arrive Holden Village, start hiking
schedule.detail: Follow Railroad Creek trail toward Hart/Lyman Lakes.

schedule.label: Reach Lower Lyman Lake, make camp

days.objective: Reach base camp at Lower Lyman Lake

days.note: An early alpine start from Lyman Lakes camp beats the afternoon thunderstorms common in this basin in summer. Leave the trail, cross the open meadow and round onto the south and southeast side of the mountain, climb to the snowfield at the foot of the flank, then follow the ledge and gully above it to a notch on the crest and scramble the final Class 2-3 rock to the summit. Reverse the same line to camp.
days.title: South-flank summit push

schedule.label: Leave camp
schedule.detail: Early start to beat afternoon thunderstorm buildup on the upper mountain.

schedule.label: Leave the trail and cross the meadow toward the south flank
Reach the notch on the crest
schedule.detail: Class 2 talus from the snowfield near 7,000 ft, then the ledge and gully to the notch; do not try to gain the cliffed southwest ridge lower down.

days.objective: Climb the south flank to the 8,096 ft summit and return to camp

days.note: Reverse the approach back down to Holden Village, timed to catch the shuttle bus to Lucerne and the afternoon Lady of the Lake departure back to Chelan. Start early with a full pack since the boat/bus connection window is tight.
days.title: Hike out + return boat/bus
days.objective: Descend to Holden Village in time for the return shuttle/ferry connection

itinerary.totalNote: A 3-day, ~21-mile round-trip backpack requiring boat + shuttle access to Holden Village, with one full day scrambling the south-side talus to the summit from a Lyman Lakes base camp (~4,500 ft total gain).

itinerary.cal: The Duckabush River Trail is open: the park's Bear Gulch Fire closures are on the Staircase side (the North Fork Skokomish, Home Sweet Home and Six Ridge trails), with no reopening date on the park's trail-conditions page updated September 14, 2026, and no Forest Service alert lists the Duckabush road or trail. The same page reports more than 50 downed trees between the trailhead and the Upper Duckabush ford — check it before planning this trip.

days.note: From the Duckabush trailhead the trail is easy for the first ~2.4 mi, then climbs steeply and loosely over Big Hump before dropping back to the river. Camp at Ten Mile Camp (1,400 ft) beside the Duckabush River; there's a privy and multiple tent sites.
days.title: Trailhead to Ten Mile Camp
days.objective: Hike in via the Duckabush River Trail to Ten Mile Camp

days.note: The trail continues along the river with overgrown, root-and-blowdown sections, then climbs in earnest toward the park's alpine zone. The final mile up to Marmot Lake / the O'Neil Pass junction is steep and exposed underfoot. Camp near O'Neil Pass (~4,950 ft) or at Marmot Lake, both of which put Mount Duckabush's south-side routes within striking distance.
days.title: Ten Mile Camp to O'Neil Pass / Marmot Lake high camp
days.objective: Continue up-valley to a high camp near O'Neil Pass or Marmot Lake, below Mount Duckabush

days.note: Drop packs at camp and head cross-country toward the peak's south side and South Ridge, mixing heather benches, talus, and short class 2-3 scrambling to the summit (6,254 ft). Route-finding is the crux more than technical difficulty; parties typically pick a line up broken rock and heather rather than a single defined trail.
days.title: Summit day: Mount Duckabush

schedule.label: Leave high camp
schedule.detail: Light daypack; leave the rest of camp set up.

schedule.label: Reach O'Neil Pass ridgeline / off-trail terrain
schedule.detail: Pick up the cross-country line toward Duckabush's south side.

schedule.label: Summit
schedule.detail: Class 2-3 scrambling on the upper mountain; watch for loose rock.

schedule.label: Back at high camp
schedule.detail: Reverse the ascent line; afternoon clouds/thunderstorms are common in summer.

days.objective: Climb Mount Duckabush from high camp and return to camp

days.note: A long, mostly-downhill day retracing the full approach — over Big Hump one more time and back to the trailhead. Many parties start before dawn to beat the heat and finish with daylight to spare.
days.title: Hike out
days.objective: Return to the Duckabush trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A 4-day, 3-night trip: roughly 43 miles and ~7,900 ft of cumulative gain round-trip, with one full day (Day 3) dedicated to the class 2-3 off-trail summit push from a high camp near O'Neil Pass/Marmot Lake.

access.fees: Duckabush Trailhead (USFS) day-use parking: $5/vehicle/day or $30 annual pass — Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency, or Digital Pass accepted (Scan & Pay only; no cash on site). No separate NPS entrance fee is charged at this backcountry-only access point.
access.notes: No separate climbing cost-recovery fee like Mount Rainier’s $82 — only the trailhead parking pass and wilderness camping permit apply.
access.rules: Overnight camping in the corridor is restricted to designated sites — 10-Mile Camp, Upper Duckabush Camp, and Marmot Lake; bear canisters are required for food storage in this zone.
access.permit: NPS wilderness camping permit required for any overnight stay past the park boundary: $8/person/night plus a non-refundable $6 reservation fee, booked on Recreation.gov. Summer-season (May 15–Oct 15) permit reservations release April 15 at 7:00 a.m. Pacific; permits can also be arranged through the Wilderness Information Center, (360) 565-3100.
access.landManager: Olympic National Forest (Duckabush Trailhead and first ~6 trail miles), transitioning to Olympic National Park / Daniel J. Evans Wilderness at the park boundary near mile 6.2.
access.land_manager: Olympic National Forest (Duckabush Trailhead and first ~6 trail miles), transitioning to Olympic National Park / Daniel J. Evans Wilderness at the park boundary near mile 6.2.
access.parking_pass: Duckabush Trailhead (USFS) day-use parking: $5/vehicle/day or $30 annual pass — Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency, or Digital Pass accepted; no separate NPS entrance fee is charged at this backcountry-only access point.
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass (or equivalent) for trailhead parking; NPS wilderness permit for any overnight travel beyond the park boundary.

overnight_permit.what: Olympic National Park wilderness permit, reserved in advance, per-night fee
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov before the trip; there are no same-day walk-up permits. Bear canisters are required in the Duckabush corridor, and fire-related closures have affected these trails, so check status first.

itinerary.cal: FR-1570 (Kindy Creek Rd) has a washout, so parking is below the road-end, adding mileage; best done June-September when the Snowking Glacier has consolidated snow and the approach trail is mostly clear.

days.note: From the FR-1570 washout parking, follow the old logging road and then the boot-beaten Kindy Ridge climbers' trail up through brush and subalpine terrain, topping out around Point 5,791 before dropping to camp near Cyclone Lake. Expect a rough, steep, brushy trail with little flat ground.
days.title: Approach to Cyclone Lake camp
days.objective: Reach camp in the meadows near Cyclone Lake (~5,350 ft)

days.note: An alpine start gets the rope team onto the Snowking Glacier while the snow is firm; climbers rope up for crevasse hazard on the ascent. After summiting, the team downclimbs to camp, breaks it down, and continues the long hike out the same day — though many parties instead camp a second night and hike out on a third day.
days.title: Snowking Glacier summit push and full hike-out

schedule.label: Leave Cyclone Lake camp
schedule.detail: Alpine start to catch firm snow on the glacier.

schedule.label: Rope up at the glacier toe
schedule.detail: Crevasse hazard begins here; team travels roped.

schedule.label: "Summit (7,433 ft)"
schedule.detail: Via the Snowking Glacier.

schedule.label: Back at camp, break down tents
schedule.detail: Some parties stop here for a second night instead of hiking out.

schedule.label: Reach trailhead/car
schedule.detail: Long day if hiking all the way out.

days.objective: Climb the Snowking Glacier to the 7,433 ft summit, then descend all the way to the car

itinerary.totalNote: A 2-day overnight trip is the standard: ~6.5 mi and ~4,700 ft to a Cyclone Lake camp on day 1, then a roped glacier summit push plus the full hike-out (~8.5 mi, ~2,700 ft gain / ~6,200 ft loss) on day 2; some parties split the hike-out into a third day.

itinerary.cal: Twin Lakes road is often snow-covered or rough into early summer; conditions are typically best August-September once the talus and rock are dry.

days.note: From the Twin Lakes trailhead, climbers go over Low Pass and High Pass and cross the basin beneath Mount Larrabee's east ridge to reach the base of the Pleiades, then scramble exposed, notoriously loose 3rd/4th class rock to the summit. Nearly everyone treats this as a long single day rather than an overnight — Twin Lakes already sits near 5,200 ft, and there's no established camp or reliable water any closer to the peaks.
days.title: Car-to-car scramble to The Pleiades

schedule.label: Leave Twin Lakes trailhead
schedule.detail: High-clearance/4WD is often needed on the final rough miles of the Twin Lakes road, especially early season.

schedule.label: Reach High Pass
schedule.detail: Traverse meadows and talus below Mount Larrabee's east ridge toward the Pleiades saddle.

schedule.label: Gain the base of the Pleiades ridge
schedule.detail: Helmets on here; the rock quality gets notably worse from this point.

schedule.label: Scramble to the summit
schedule.detail: Exposed 3rd/4th class climbing on chossy blocks and a short slab pitch to the 'goat ledge'; parties note this stretch commonly takes 2-3x longer than expected.

schedule.label: Summit
schedule.detail: Highpoint of the group at 7,371 ft.

schedule.label: Down-climb and return to trailhead
schedule.detail: Mostly down-climbing — reverse the ascent line carefully, with a short rappel at a steep step or two; loose rock makes the descent rockfall-prone for parties below.

days.objective: Reach the high point of The Pleiades via the Twin Lakes / High Pass approach

itinerary.totalNote: A long, technical single day: roughly 7.5 miles round trip with about 3,200 ft of gain/loss, but slow going (9-11 hrs car to car) due to sustained loose 3rd/4th class scrambling near the summit.

itinerary.cal: Boston Basin sites require winning NPS's early-access permit lottery; Cascade River Road access to the trailhead opens on a variable date each summer depending on winter road damage.

days.note: Hike in from the trailhead to a camp near 6,400 ft in Boston Basin, from which the Northwest Face's approach notches are reachable.
days.title: Approach to Boston Basin camp
days.objective: Establish camp below the peak

days.note: From camp, work up and over intermediate notches and rappel into the glacier basins below the face — a more complex, committing approach than the standard routes. Climb the face proper to the upper mountain, tag the summit, then descend the West Ridge couloir back to camp.
days.title: Northwest Face to summit, descend West Ridge couloir

schedule.label: Reach first notch/glacier rappel
schedule.detail: Route crosses two notches and two glacier basins that are hard to exit

schedule.label: Summit
schedule.detail: Timing varies widely with crevasse/snow conditions

schedule.label: Descend West Ridge couloir
schedule.detail: Standard descent back into Boston Basin

days.objective: Climb the Northwest Face and descend the standard couloir

itinerary.totalNote: A 2-day trip: hike in and camp in Boston Basin, then a long, complex ~12 hr face day (multiple notches and glacier basins) to the summit, descending the standard West Ridge couloir; very fit parties have linked it car-to-car in ~17 hrs.

road.name: Cascade River Road to Boston Basin Trailhead
road.status: Open seasonally
road.driveNote: From Marblemount via Cascade River Road to the Boston Basin/climber's trailhead.
road.seasonalGate: Gated/snow-covered in winter and spring

itinerary.cal: The Shannon Creek/FR-1152 approach road usually isn't reliably snow-free and driveable until late June; late July-August is prime season for stable glacier crossing and a straightforward rappel off the summit pyramid.

days.note: A well-graded trail climbs through old growth and subalpine meadows onto Shannon Ridge, then across talus and heather to a flat camp near the toe of the glacier. Most parties budget 5-6 hours.
days.title: Approach to high camp
days.objective: Reach high camp on the Sulphide Glacier

days.note: Rope up before dawn and cross the glacier's crevasses to the base of the summit pyramid, then scramble and rappel to the true summit. Reverse the whole thing back to camp - a long but non-technical day for a roped/glacier-travel party.
days.title: Summit day

schedule.label: Rope up, leave camp
schedule.detail: Cross onto the glacier while it's still firm.

schedule.label: Reach base of summit pyramid
schedule.detail: Crevasse navigation on the upper glacier.

schedule.label: Summit
schedule.detail: Scramble/short rappel off the pyramid.

schedule.label: Back at camp
schedule.detail: Reverse rappel and glacier crossing.

days.objective: Climb the Sulphide Glacier and summit pyramid, return to camp

days.note: Retrace Shannon Ridge back down to the car; a straightforward 4-hour descent.
days.title: Hike out
days.objective: Break camp and hike back to the trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A 3-day, 2-night standard trip: about 16 miles round trip and roughly 6,600 ft of total gain; fit independent parties sometimes compress it into a strong 2-day (hike-in-then-summit-and-out) trip instead.

road.name: Baker Lake Highway (FS Road 11) to FS 1152 / 1152014
road.status: Gravel forest roads, normally passable to high-clearance vehicles in summer
road.driveNote: About 28 miles of forest-road driving from SR 20 to the trailhead

itinerary.cal: Pasayten Wilderness requires only a free self-issue permit at the trailhead (no quota); the Andrews Creek approach is typically snow-free and drivable July through September.

days.note: A long, steady approach on the Andrews Creek Trail through forest and subalpine meadows into the Pasayten Wilderness, ending at Upper Cathedral Lake, the standard base camp for the peak. Self-issue a free wilderness permit at the trailhead kiosk before starting.
days.title: Backpack to Upper Cathedral Lake

schedule.label: Leave Andrews Creek Trailhead
schedule.detail: Self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead register.

schedule.label: Pass Spanish Camp / Cathedral Pass junction
Arrive Upper Cathedral Lake
schedule.detail: Set up camp and scout the buttress across the basin.

days.objective: Reach high camp at Upper Cathedral Lake (7,380 ft)

days.note: Alpine start for the short approach to the base of the buttress, then 10 pitches of sustained hand and finger cracks on excellent granite to the 8,606 ft summit. Descend via the 3rd-class scramble route, including a short, exposed Class 4 gap crossing, back to camp.
days.title: Southeast Buttress summit day

schedule.label: Rack up at base of route
schedule.detail: ~40 min approach from the lake.

schedule.label: Top out on summit
schedule.detail: 7-9 hrs of climbing depending on party size and conditions.

schedule.label: Begin descent
schedule.detail: 3rd-class scramble trending west/southwest, including the exposed Class 4 notch ('leap of faith').

days.objective: Climb the SE Buttress (10 pitches, 5.9+/5.10a) and return to camp

days.note: Many parties build in a layover day at Upper Cathedral Lake to recover and take advantage of being deep in the Pasayten -- a common add-on is the easy 3rd-class scramble up nearby Amphitheater Mountain or Deacon Peak. Skip this day entirely for a faster 4-day trip.
days.title: Rest day / optional bonus summit
days.objective: Recover, or scramble Amphitheater Mountain or Deacon Peak

days.note: Retrace the Andrews Creek Trail back to the trailhead, losing the elevation gained on Day 1.
days.title: Hike out
days.objective: Return to Andrews Creek Trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A 4-5 day trip: roughly 36 miles round-trip and 4,350 ft of approach gain on the Andrews Creek Trail, plus an 8-11 hour, 10-pitch 5.9+/5.10a summit day from Upper Cathedral Lake camp; many parties add a rest or bonus-summit day.

road.name: Forest Road 51 (Chewuch River Road) to Andrews Creek Trailhead
road.status: paved the whole way: about 23 miles from Winthrop, the first ~6 on Okanogan County Rd 1213/West Chewuch Rd and the rest on Forest Road 51 to the trailhead, where the pavement ends
road.driveNote: From Winthrop: WA-20 to West Chewuch Road (Okanogan County Rd 1213), follow it ~6 miles to Forest Road 51, then continue on pavement to the trailhead, about 23 miles from Winthrop in all (el. 3,050 ft). No high clearance needed in normal summer conditions.
road.seasonalGate: Upper FR 51 is typically snowed in through late spring; usually passable by early-mid summer — confirm current conditions with the Methow Valley Ranger District before driving in.

itinerary.cal: Westside Road is gated at Dry Creek most of the year, adding about 3.8 miles of road walking to the approach.

days.note: From the Westside Road gate, walk the road to Round Pass, then the South Puyallup River Trail and Wonderland Trail to a camp around 6,000 ft.
days.title: Long approach to St. Andrews Park
days.objective: Reach a camp near St. Andrews Park

days.note: Climb the Puyallup Cleaver past Tokaloo Spire, then traverse north across the Puyallup and South Mowich glaciers to a high camp on the South Mowich Glacier (~9,600 ft).
days.title: Move to high camp
days.objective: Reach a high camp below Sunset Amphitheater

days.note: Climb steep gullies and snowfields through Sunset Amphitheater — in a dry year a thin choss-wall/gully transition on the ridge can need an improvised belay or stop the climb — then descend a standard route.
days.title: Summit day

schedule.label: Gully/choss-wall transition
schedule.detail: Reported thin in dry years, sometimes needing an improvised belay

days.objective: Climb the ridge through Sunset Amphitheater to the summit

days.note: Descend to Camp Schurman or Camp Muir depending on the descent route, then arrange transport back to Westside Road since the standard descents exit on the opposite side of the mountain.
days.title: Exit
days.objective: Hike out the far side and shuttle back to Westside Road

itinerary.totalNote: A remote 4-day trip (~11,500 ft gain) on the mountain's least-visited side; plan a car shuttle since the standard descent exits far from the Westside Road start.

road.name: Westside Road
road.status: Gravel; open to vehicles for only the first ~3 miles to the Dry Creek trailhead (long-term flood damage near Tahoma Creek closed the rest to cars), then it's foot/bike travel to Round Pass and beyond
road.driveNote: Park at the Dry Creek gate and hike the remaining road/climbers' route toward Tokaloo Rock and the Puyallup Glacier.
road.seasonalGate: Vehicle-accessible section (to Dry Creek) typically open May–November; the road beyond Dry Creek has been closed to vehicles for years and is hiked or biked
